Selling online
Traffic but no sales? Work through these seven places, in order
Traffic means people reach your shop’s door. No sales means that somewhere between the door and the till, they turn around and walk out. This article maps that path.
21 November 2026·8 min read·The dadmor team

In this article

  1. First things first: is the problem traffic, or the shop itself?
  2. Check one: do they trust you within ten seconds?
  3. Check two: does your product page answer without a DM?
  4. Check three: does your checkout survive a cheap phone?
  5. Check four: how slow is it on real Iranian internet?
  6. Check five: why should the customer buy today?
  7. Check six: does anyone call the abandoned cart back?
  8. Check seven: do you even know where the customer leaves?
  9. The bottom line

Summary

  1. Most shops that say “we have traffic but no sales” do not have a traffic problem. They have one specific broken place on the path between walking in and paying.
  2. Work through the seven places in this order: trust, the product page’s answers, checkout on a cheap phone, real speed, a reason to buy today, abandoned cart follow up, and measuring.
  3. Each check comes with a test that takes a few minutes, tonight, on your own phone. Do not guess. Test, then fix that one place.

She opens her stats: yesterday, 417 visits. She opens her orders: zero. Almost every online shop owner has lived this scene, and the first guess is nearly always the same: “I must need more advertising.”

Most of the time, no. Advertising pours more people into the same shop. If they turn around and leave somewhere inside it, advertising just makes the leaving more crowded. Good traffic with no sales means the path between the door and the till is broken in one place. Your job is to find that place, not to open the traffic tap wider.
So we walk that path in order: seven stations, from the moment someone arrives to after payment. At each one we tell you what to look at, and what test to run tonight, on your own phone.
First things first: is the problem traffic, or the shop itself?

If your traffic is very low, this article is not for you yet. People have to reach the shop first. But if tens or hundreds arrive every day and almost nobody buys, traffic is not your problem. In small shops, one or two purchases from every hundred real visitors is nothing strange. Absolute zero, week after week, means one place on the path is shut.
Now we go in order. Run each station’s test, then move to the next.
Check one: do they trust you within ten seconds?

A new customer does not know you. In the first seconds they have one question only: is this place real? They answer it from what they can see: a real phone number and address that are easy to find, the electronic trust symbol and a payment gateway whose name they know, an about page showing a real person behind the shop, and prices and terms that are hidden nowhere.

Tonight’s test: put the site on a phone in front of someone who does not know your shop. After ten seconds, take the phone back and ask: would you pay by card here? Listen to the answer exactly as it comes. Do not explain anything.
A customer rarely says no out loud. They just quietly turn around and leave. Your job is to find the exact step where they turn back.
Check two: does your product page answer without a DM?

Every question the product page does not answer becomes a DM, or a lost customer. These four must be clear without messaging anyone and without hunting: the final price, the cost and time of shipping, the return conditions, and whether it is in stock. A real product photo and a description that helps someone choose get decided on that same page.
Tonight’s test: open one product page and time how long it takes to find the shipping cost. Longer than a minute? Your customer gives up in exactly the same place.
Check three: does your checkout survive a cheap phone?

Most of your customers buy on mid range and cheap Android phones, not on your office phone and your office internet. A checkout with too many steps, a discount code that throws a strange error, or a payment page that falls apart on mobile loses the customer at the exact moment of paying.

Tonight’s test: take the cheapest phone in the house, switch to mobile data, and buy something from your own shop, all the way to the payment receipt. Everywhere you paused or frowned, your customer has already left.
Check four: how slow is it on real Iranian internet?

Everyone tests speed on home or office wifi. Your customer buys in the street, on mobile data. Heavy product photos, and a page where you stare at white for several seconds just to see the price, mean a silent goodbye on that connection.

Tonight’s test: turn wifi off and open your best selling product page on mobile data. If the price and the buy button take more than a few seconds to show up, lighten the photos first. It is usually the cheapest repair a shop has.
Check five: why should the customer buy today?

“I will buy later” in practice means I will not buy. Buying today needs one real reason: free shipping above a clear amount, stock that is genuinely low, a gift on the first order, or a delivery date you actually know. Real means it is still true tomorrow, exactly as you said it today. Fake countdowns and a permanent “only two left” destroy the trust from check one as well.
Tonight’s test: read your product page like a stranger and ask: if I do not buy today, what do I lose? If the answer is “nothing”, your customer has worked out exactly the same thing.
Check six: does anyone call the abandoned cart back?

Most carts get abandoned. That is normal, in every shop in the world. The shops that sell are the ones that do not treat abandonment as the end of the story: one reminder SMS or email in the first few hours, and for pricier carts, one short human phone call. A customer who reached the till is your warmest customer. Saying goodbye to them in silence is a waste.
Tonight’s test: build a cart with your own number and abandon it. Over the next twenty four hours, does anything reach you? If not, your customers are hearing nothing either.
Check seven: do you even know where the customer leaves?

If there is no analytics tool on your site, or you never look at it, you are repairing in the dark. You do not need to become a data scientist. Three numbers are enough: which product page gets the most visits, at which checkout step the biggest drop happens, and whether customers mostly come on mobile or desktop. Those numbers tell you which check to take seriously first.
Tonight’s test: answer this without guessing: which is your most visited product page, and how many sales did it make last month? If you do not know, your first step is here, not advertising.
The bottom line

Good traffic and zero sales come down to one sentence: people arrive, and somewhere they turn back. You will not find that place by guessing. You find it with these seven tests, and fixing it usually costs less than fresh advertising. And if the tests show the problem is the shop building itself, its checkout, product pages and speed, then it is rebuilding time. On the website building page you can see how we build a shop, and the project estimator gives you the number before any conversation.

Frequently asked questions

How do I know the problem is traffic or the site itself?

If your daily traffic is decent but sales have sat near zero for several weeks, the problem is almost always inside the site. If traffic was low from the start, fix traffic first. This article is for when people come, and do not buy.

Which check should I do first?

Follow the article’s order: trust and the product page first, because that is where most people drop, then checkout and speed. Each test takes a few minutes, and you do not have to do all seven in one night.

Should I buy advertising to get sales moving?

Advertising into a shop with a broken checkout just delivers more visitors who do not buy. Find the drop and fix it first. Then the same advertising, on the same budget, starts producing sales.

Does the trust symbol alone fix sales?

No. The symbol is one trust signal among several, and it only means something next to a real contact number, an about page and clear buying terms. No badge makes up for a broken checkout and a half finished product page.
